lead: A whole-body plethysmograph is a rigid sealed box, about 600 L, in which the subject sits and breathes through a mouthpiece with a shutter. When the subject pants against the closed shutter, the trapped lung gas is squeezed and stretched; Boyle's law turns the tiny box-pressure swing and the larger mouth-pressure swing into the volume of gas in the chest. That gives functional residual capacity and residual volume, which a spirometer cannot measure. With the shutter open, the same box gives alveolar pressure and so airway resistance.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 for lung-volume names and Chapter 2.6 for flow, pressure and airway resistance.

sections.h3: The sealed box and two pressure signals

blocks.text: The box is rigid and sealed, so the gas inside has a fixed mass. Two transducers record the signals: one measures mouth pressure, P<sub>mouth</sub>, at the mouthpiece; the other measures box pressure, P<sub>box</sub>. A pneumotachometer in the mouthpiece measures flow. A small piston pump on the box wall is pushed in and out by a known volume to calibrate the box: it gives K<sub>box</sub>, the box-volume change per unit of box pressure, for example 400 mL per cm H₂O.

With the shutter closed the subject pants gently at about 1 Hz. Breathing-muscle effort compresses the lung gas a little on each push and expands it on each pull; the chest grows and shrinks by the same tiny volume ΔV, and the box gas around the subject changes volume by the same ΔV the other way, so P<sub>box</sub> swings. Because the airway is shut there is no flow, so the mouth pressure equals the alveolar pressure. Panting is used because it is fast: the lung gas stays at body temperature and saturated (isothermal), and the box gas has no time to exchange heat with the walls, which the piston calibration already allows for.

sections.h3: Thoracic gas volume, FRC and residual volume

blocks.text: Apply Boyle's law to the trapped lung gas. Only the dry gas obeys it, because the water vapour pressure stays at 47 mmHg at 37 °C however hard the gas is squeezed. If the lung volume V changes by ΔV while alveolar pressure changes by ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>, P V = (P + ΔP)(V − ΔV), which for small changes gives:
V<sub>tg</sub> = ΔV × (P<sub>B</sub> − P<sub>H₂O</sub>) / ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>,   ΔV = K<sub>box</sub> × ΔP<sub>box</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>tg</sub> is the thoracic gas volume; ΔV is the lung volume change read from the calibrated box; P<sub>B</sub> is barometric pressure and P<sub>H₂O</sub> = 47 mmHg, both converted to cm H₂O (760 mmHg = 1033 cm H₂O, 47 mmHg = 64 cm H₂O, so P<sub>B</sub> − P<sub>H₂O</sub> ≈ 970 cm H₂O at sea level); ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> and ΔP<sub>box</sub> are the peak-to-peak swings in cm H₂O.

blocks.text: If the shutter closes at the end of a quiet breath out, V<sub>tg</sub> is the functional residual capacity, FRC. A spirometer in the same sitting gives the expiratory reserve volume ERV and the vital capacity VC, and the rest follows: RV = FRC − ERV and TLC = RV + VC. The ratio RV/TLC, normally about 0.25 to 0.35 in young adults, rises with air trapping in COPD and asthma.

The gas methods measure only gas that talks to the airway. In helium dilution the subject rebreathes from a closed spirometer of volume V₁ holding helium at fraction C₁; helium is not absorbed, so after mixing C₁V₁ = C₂(V₁ + FRC) and FRC = V₁(C₁ − C₂)/C₂, with carbon dioxide absorbed and oxygen added as it is used. In nitrogen washout the subject breathes pure oxygen and all exhaled gas is collected until the nitrogen is gone; FRC = (volume collected × its nitrogen fraction) ÷ the starting alveolar nitrogen fraction, about 0.80. Gas trapped behind closed airways is missed by both but is counted by the box, so in COPD the box FRC is the larger.

sections.h3: Airway resistance with the shutter open

blocks.text: With the shutter open the subject keeps panting, now through the pneumotachometer. To drive air out, alveolar pressure must rise above mouth pressure; that compresses the alveolar gas slightly, and the box sees it as a pressure swing. The closed-shutter run has already shown how many cm H₂O of alveolar pressure go with each unit of box pressure, so the box swing in the open run can be turned into alveolar pressure without any probe in the lung:

blocks.where: R<sub>aw</sub> is airway resistance in cm H₂O per L/s; the first ratio is the slope of the closed-shutter trace; the second is the box swing per unit flow V̇ (in L/s) in the open-shutter trace. The box units cancel.

blocks.text: Normal adult airway resistance is roughly 0.6 to 2.4 cm H₂O per L/s; higher values suggest obstruction. Conductance is G<sub>aw</sub> = 1/R<sub>aw</sub>. Because airways widen as the lung fills, resistance falls at larger lung volumes, so reports also give specific values that remove that effect: sR<sub>aw</sub> = R<sub>aw</sub> × V<sub>tg</sub> and sG<sub>aw</sub> = G<sub>aw</sub> / V<sub>tg</sub>. Write resistance as cm H₂O per L/s, not cm H₂O/L.

examples.question: A subject sits in a body box whose piston calibration gives K<sub>box</sub> = 400 mL per cm H₂O. Barometric pressure is 760 mmHg. With the shutter closed at the end of a quiet breath out, the subject pants: mouth pressure swings by 9.7 cm H₂O and box pressure by 0.075 cm H₂O. Spirometry gives ERV = 1.2 L and VC = 4.0 L. With the shutter open, a flow swing of 1.0 L/s goes with a box swing of 0.0116 cm H₂O. Find (a) the thoracic gas volume, (b) RV and TLC, (c) airway resistance and specific airway conductance.
steps: (a) Lung volume change: ΔV = K<sub>box</sub> × ΔP<sub>box</sub> = 400 × 0.075 = 30 mL.
Dry-gas pressure: P<sub>B</sub> − P<sub>H₂O</sub> = (760 − 47) mmHg = 713 mmHg × 1.36 = 970 cm H₂O.
V<sub>tg</sub> = ΔV × 970 / ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> = 30 mL × 970 / 9.7 = 3000 mL = 3.0 L. The shutter closed at end-expiration, so this is FRC.
(c) Closed-shutter slope: ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>/ΔP<sub>box</sub> = 9.7/0.075 = 129.3. Open-shutter: ΔP<sub>box</sub>/V̇ = 0.0116 per L/s.
R<sub>aw</sub> = 129.3 × 0.0116 = 1.50 cm H₂O per L/s, inside the normal range of about 0.6 to 2.4.
G<sub>aw</sub> = 1/1.50 = 0.667 L/s per cm H₂O; sG<sub>aw</sub> = 0.667/3.0 = 0.22 per s per cm H₂O.
examples.answer: V<sub>tg</sub> = FRC = 3.0 L; RV = 1.8 L, TLC = 5.8 L; R<sub>aw</sub> = 1.50 cm H₂O per L/s (normal) and sG<sub>aw</sub> = 0.22 per s per cm H₂O.

examples.question: Helium dilution in the same subject: a closed spirometer holds 5.0 L of gas with 10.0 % helium. After a few minutes of rebreathing from FRC the helium reads 6.25 %. Find FRC and compare it with the box value.
steps: Helium is conserved: C₁V₁ = C₂(V₁ + FRC), so FRC = V₁(C₁ − C₂)/C₂.
The helium value equals the box value, 3.0 L, so no gas is trapped behind closed airways. In COPD the box would read higher.
examples.answer: FRC = 3.0 L by helium dilution, the same as the plethysmograph, so there is no trapped gas.

traps: Using the box swing as if it were a volume: ΔP<sub>box</sub> becomes ΔV only through the piston calibration K<sub>box</sub>.
Forgetting water vapour: Boyle's law uses P<sub>B</sub> − 47 mmHg, about 970 cm H₂O at sea level, not 1033 cm H₂O.
Mixing FRC and residual volume: V<sub>tg</sub> at an end-expiration shutter closure is FRC; RV = FRC − ERV.
Expecting helium dilution to agree in COPD: gas trapped behind closed airways never meets the helium, so the gas method reads lower than the box.
Writing airway resistance in cm H₂O/L instead of cm H₂O per L/s.

quiz.q: What does a whole-body plethysmograph measure when the shutter is closed at end-expiration?
quiz.a: The thoracic gas volume at that moment, which is the functional residual capacity, from Boyle's law using the mouth and box pressure swings.

quiz.q: Why is the panting manoeuvre used against the closed shutter?
quiz.a: Panting is fast and small: the lung gas stays isothermal and saturated, so Boyle's law applies; the glottis stays open, so mouth pressure equals alveolar pressure; and slow drifts in box temperature do not build up.

quiz.q: A box has K<sub>box</sub> = 500 mL per cm H₂O. Panting gives ΔP<sub>box</sub> = 0.06 cm H₂O and ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> = 9.7 cm H₂O at sea level. Find V<sub>tg</sub>.
V<sub>tg</sub> = 3.5 L at end-expiration, ERV = 1.1 L and VC = 4.2 L. Find RV, TLC and RV/TLC.
quiz.a: RV = 3.5 − 1.1 = 2.4 L; TLC = 2.4 + 4.2 = 6.6 L; RV/TLC = 2.4/6.6 = 0.36, at the top of the normal range.

quiz.q: Why does helium dilution read a lower FRC than the body box in severe COPD?
quiz.a: Helium reaches only gas that is open to the airways. Gas trapped behind closed airways is not diluted but is still compressed during panting, so the box counts it and the helium method misses it.

quiz.q: The closed-shutter slope ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>/ΔP<sub>box</sub> is 120 and the open-shutter run gives ΔP<sub>box</sub>/V̇ = 0.025 per L/s. Find R<sub>aw</sub> and comment.
quiz.a: R<sub>aw</sub> = 120 × 0.025 = 3.0 cm H₂O per L/s, above the normal range of about 0.6 to 2.4, which suggests airway obstruction; repeat after a bronchodilator to see whether it is reversible.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern body boxes compute V<sub>tg</sub> and R<sub>aw</sub> breath by breath and correct the thermal drift of the box gas, and forced oscillation measures resistance without a box, which helps children. Search next for body plethysmography, specific airway conductance and multiple-breath nitrogen washout.
